summary: Defines a MIB for controlling a Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement meter, especially for specifying which flows to measure. It also provides an efficient way to retrieve flow data from the meter using SNMP. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: A meter is like a counter at a road that tracks cars. This MIB is the remote control for telling it which cars to count.

subtitle: The SNMP interface for configuring a network traffic meter and efficiently reading the flows it counts.

tldr.problem: A network traffic flow meter needs a standard way for managers to tell it which flows to measure and for meter readers to collect the results, without a huge number of SNMP exchanges.
tldr.mechanism: The Meter MIB defines control tables for rule sets, meter readers and managers, a flow table with 64-bit counters and time-based indexes, a rule table of packet-matching rules, and a data package table that returns chosen attributes of a flow as one BER-encoded value.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2064 and has not itself been obsoleted. Security depends on protecting both SNMP access and the metering interfaces.

today: RFC 2720 is a Proposed Standard from October 1999 that obsoletes RFC 2064, and the unit metadata records no later RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What the Meter MIB Is For
sections.content:
The RTFM (Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement) architecture describes network traffic as flows, defined by the values of address attributes, and measured by a traffic meter. This memo defines the Management Information Base (MIB) used to control such a meter, above all to say which flows to measure, and a way to fetch flow data from it with SNMP.

The architecture has three entities. Meters watch traffic and build a table of flow records. Meter readers collect the flow data from meters. Managers oversee the meters and meter readers.

The MIB is called basic: it gives more than enough information for everyday measurement and can be extended by adding attributes. It is written in SMIv2, and a SMIv1 version can be produced by translation, except for objects that need Counter64.
sections.plainLanguage: The counter by the road has three kinds of helpers: the counter itself, people who come to read the totals, and a boss who decides what to count.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Organised
sections.content:
All objects live in one subtree, flowMIB, registered as mib-2 40. The MIB has four parts: control, data, rules and conformance statements. Times inside the meter are its Uptime, in centiseconds since the meter started.

Flows are identified by attributes of each end-point, such as network addresses at each layer of the protocol stack and optional subscriber ids that can name an accountable entity. The attributes are grouped into adjacent (link), peer (network) and transport layers, with a source and a destination version of each.

The flow table keeps 64-bit counters for octets and packets in each direction, plus the times a flow was first and last active. Because every flow keeps counts both ways, one record covers traffic from source to destination and from destination to source.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything about the counter is stored in one big filing cabinet with four drawers: settings, results, counting rules and a checklist of what it must support.

sections.title: Control Tables for Rule Sets, Readers and Managers
sections.content:
Control is done through three tables, built like those in the RMON2 MIB.

  • Rule set info. A manager creates a row in flowRuleSetInfoTable, sets flowRuleInfoSize to the number of rules, downloads the rules, then sets flowRuleInfoStatus to active(1). The rule set is then available but not running, and it can no longer be changed.
  • Manager info. To run a rule set, a manager creates a row in flowManagerInfoTable and points its current or standby rule set at it. Setting both to 0 stops it. A standby rule set takes over when the flow table reaches the row's high water mark, and should have a coarser reporting granularity.
  • Meter reader info. A reader that wants reliable collection creates a row in flowReaderInfoTable naming the rule set, and writes flowReaderLastTime at the start of each pass. The meter will not recover a flow's memory until every registered reader has collected it.

A few general variables are set by a single master manager. flowInactivityTimeout defaults to 600 seconds and defines when a flow becomes idle. flowFloodMark defaults to 95 percent and says how full the flow table may get before the meter acts to avoid running out of resources. flowFloodMode shows the meter has passed it. flowInterfaceSampleRate counts 1/Nth of the packets on an interface, where 1 counts all and 0 ignores the interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss writes a list of counting rules, then says which list to use. Readers sign a guest book so the counter does not throw away old counts before everyone has copied them.

sections.title: Reading Flow Data Efficiently
sections.content:
Reading the flow table one row at a time would work but needs many protocol exchanges. Instead the flow table is indexed by rule set, a TimeFilter (from RMON2) and flow index, so a reader can use GetNext or GetBulk to fetch only flows that changed since a given time and that came from a given rule set.

The data package table, flowDataPackageTable, goes further. It is logically a four-dimensional array indexed by a package selector, rule set, activity time and flow number. The selector is a length octet followed by a list of attribute numbers. The returned flowPackageData holds the values of those attributes for one flow as a single sequence encoded with the Basic Encoding Rules. This lets a reader pick up everything it needs in one object, which together with SNMPv2 GetBulk makes table scans efficient.

The indexes are stateless, so several meter readers can work independently with different intervals. The cost is that two readers never see exactly the same counts, which the RFC says is acceptable over long periods such as 15-minute collections across a day. A true snapshot can be had by switching between two identical rule sets with different numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of asking about each car one detail at a time, you ask for a short summary card for each car, and only for cars seen since your last visit.

sections.title: The Rule Table
sections.content:
The rule table holds all the rule sets a meter can use. Each rule has a flowRuleSelector (the attribute to test), a flowRuleMask, a flowRuleMatchedValue, a flowRuleAction and a flowRuleParameter. If the selected attribute ANDed with the mask equals the matched value, the action runs. Otherwise processing moves to the next rule. A zero mask always succeeds, and a null selector always succeeds.

Actions are opcodes for the meter's Packet Matching Engine, such as ignore, count, return, gosub, assign and goto. Their details are in the RTFM architecture document, not here. Subroutines let a manager greatly reduce the number of rules needed to watch a large network. Five meter variables, v1 to v5, can hold an attribute number and be set by an assign action.

The RFC advises that although one rule could be changed, it is much safer to download a complete new rule set, and a rule set that is referenced by a manager row cannot be changed at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule is a simple question: does this car look like the one I want? If yes, do the thing, such as count it. If no, try the next rule down the list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access, all the control objects, and the flow table can be sensitive, so even read access should be controlled and possibly encrypted. SNMPv1 is not a secure environment. The RFC recommends the SNMPv3 User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575). Views can also split one meter into virtual meters, one for each manager.

An attacker must not be able to write any meter variable. Suggested protections are physical separation of the control network, application-layer security (community strings are only clear-text passwords), and lower-layer encryption, with separate interfaces for control and metering where possible.

The RFC also describes attempts to evade the meter. A port scan creates many new flows and can push the meter into flood mode. A counter wrap attack sends enough packets to wrap counters between readings, which the 64-bit counters in this MIB largely avoid. Reading the meter often enough reduces both problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted people should hold the remote control, and the counter should be hard to trick into missing cars or filling its notebook with fake ones.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2064
sections.content:
This memo replaces RFC 2064. The main changes are greater use of textual conventions for address types, new testable computed attributes and a MatchingStoD attribute, and a writable flood mode so a manager can return the meter to normal operation. More control variables were added, and 64-bit counters replaced 32-bit ones in the flow table.

flowDataRuleSet became an index, so a reader can collect only rows made by one rule set. The new data package table replaced the use of the Column Activity Table, which made it hard to collect all data for a flow in one SNMP request. That table and some other objects are marked deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an updated edition. Counters hold bigger numbers, and there is a faster way to read the results.
